text: Marina Abramović, born November 30, 1946, in Belgrade, PR Serbia, FPR Yugoslavia, is a Serbian conceptual and performance artist. Her work investigates body art, endurance art, the relationship between performer and audience, the limits of the body, and the possibilities of the mind. Active for over four decades, she refers to herself as the "grandmother of performance art" and pioneered a new notion of artistic identity by involving observers, focusing on confronting pain, blood, and the physical limits of the body. In 2007, she founded the Marina Abramović Institute (MAI), a non-profit foundation for performance art. Abramović was raised by her grandparents until she was six years old; her grandmother was deeply religious, and she spent her childhood in church following her grandmother's rituals. When she was six, her brother was born, and she began living with her parents, taking piano, French, and English lessons, though she did not take art lessons and only enjoyed painting as a child. Life under her mother's strict supervision was difficult; her mother beat her for "supposedly showing off," and she described being under military-style control until age 29, which limited her performances to before 10 p.m. In a 1998 interview, she recalled her parents' terrible marriage, citing an incident when her father smashed 12 champagne glasses and left the house as the most horrible moment of her childhood. She studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Belgrade from 1965 to 1970 and completed post-graduate studies in the art class of Krsto Hegedušić at the Academy of Fine Arts in Zagreb in 1972. From 1973 to 1975, she taught at the Academy of Fine Arts in Novi Sad while launching her first solo performances. In 1976, after marrying Neša Paripović (between 1970 and 1976), she moved to Amsterdam permanently to perform there. From 1990 to 1995, she was a visiting professor at the Académie des Beaux-Arts in Paris and the Berlin University of the Arts; from 1992 to 1996, she taught at the Hochschule für bildende Künste Hamburg, and from 1997 to 2004, she was a professor for performance art at the Hochschule für bildende Künste Braunschweig. In her 1973 Edinburgh performance, she used ten knives and two tape recorders to explore ritual and gesture, cutting herself ten times and replaying the recordings to replicate the movements, thus examining the physical and mental limits of the body. In another performance, she lit a large petroleum-drenched star on fire, cutting her nails, toenails, and hair, throwing the clippings into the flames, and leaping into the center of the pentagram after losing consciousness due to lack of oxygen, which the audience initially failed to notice. She later commented that losing consciousness meant she could no longer be present and perform. Prompted by this, she created Rhythm 2 in 1974, which involved ingesting medications to induce muscle contractions and loss of bodily control while remaining aware, followed by a calming medication, lasting five hours. In Rhythm 4, performed at Galleria Diagramma in Milan, she knelt naked in a room with a high-power industrial fan, attempting to breathe in as much air as possible, and soon lost consciousness. To prevent audience interference, she had the cameraman focus only on her face, but after several minutes of unconsciousness, the cameraman stopped and called for help. In a 1976 performance in Naples, she placed 72 objects on a table for the audience to use as they wished, including a rose, feather, honey, whip, olive oil, scissors, scalpel, gun, and a single bullet. For six hours, the audience manipulated her body, leading to her being stripped, attacked, and devalued into an image she described as the "Madonna, mother, and whore," with one person aiming a gun at her head and others cutting her clothes. She later stated that if the audience is left to act, they can kill her and that she felt deeply violated. Abramović defines her identity in contrast to that of spectators, blurring roles to reveal collective human experiences and truths, and her work also explores the objectification of the female body, testing the limits of danger and exhaustion. In 1976, she met Uwe Laysiepen, known as Ulay, with whom she began a collaborative relationship exploring ego and artistic identity, creating "relation works" characterized by movement, change, and "art vital," forming a collective identity called "The Other" and speaking of themselves as parts of a "two-headed body." They dressed and behaved like twins, creating a relationship of complete trust, reducing individual identities. Critics have interpreted their work as a hermaphroditic state, but Abramović rejects this, emphasizing her focus on the body as a unit of individuality, rooted in her parents' military pasts, and their exploration of extreme states of consciousness and architectural space. Between 1981 and 1987, they performed Nightsea Crossing in twenty-two performances, sitting silently across from each other for seven hours a day. In 1988, after years of tension, they embarked on a spiritual journey to end their relationship, walking the Great Wall of China from opposite ends—Ulay from the Gobi Desert and Abramović from the Yellow Sea—each walking 2500 km to meet in the middle and say goodbye. She conceived the walk in a dream and described it as a dramatic, human, and film-like ending, emphasizing solitude. The journey took eight years to gain Chinese government permission, and by then, their relationship had dissolved. At her 2010 MoMA retrospective, she performed The Artist Is Present, sharing a period of silence with each visitor who sat in front of her; when Ulay arrived, she reached out to him across the table, an emotional moment that went viral. In November 2015, Ulay sued Abramović, claiming she had paid him insufficient royalties under a 1999 contract covering sales of their joint works, and in September 2016, a Dutch court ordered her to pay €250,000 in royalties, plus over €23,000 in legal costs, finding that Ulay was entitled to 20% net royalties as specified in the contract, and requiring her to credit all works from 1976 to 1980 as "Ulay/Abramović" and from 1981 to 1988 as "Abramović/Ulay." Cleaning the Mirror consisted of five monitors showing Abramović scrubbing a grimy human skeleton in her lap, with each monitor dedicated to a different body part—head, pelvis, ribs, hands, feet—each with its own sound, creating overlaps. As the skeleton became cleaner, Abramović became covered in the grayish dirt. The three-hour performance, including Cleaning the Mirror #1 at MoMA, #2 at Oxford University (90 minutes), and #3 at the Pitt Rivers Museum (five hours), is filled with metaphors of Tibetan death rites. In 1996, she worked with Jacob Samuel to produce a cookbook of "aphrodisiac recipes" called Spirit Cooking, with evocative instructions such as "13,000 grams of jealousy" and "mix fresh breast milk with fresh sperm milk," inspired by the belief that ghosts feed on emotions, sound, and light. In 1997, she created a multimedia Spirit Cooking installation at Zerynthia Associazione per l'Arte Contemporanea in Rome, featuring white gallery walls with "enigmatically violent recipe instructions" painted in pig's blood, described by Alexxa Gotthardt as a comment on humanity's reliance on ritual to organize and legitimize life. Spirit Cooking later evolved into a dinner party entertainment for collectors, donors, and friends. In a performance involving the scrubbing of thousands of bloody cow bones over four days, Abramović earned the Golden Lion award at the Venice Biennale. She created Balkan Baroque as a response to the Yugoslav Wars, recalling that other artists reacted immediately, but she could not create work soon due to the emotional impact. She returned to Belgrade, interviewed her mother, father, and a rat-catcher, and incorporated these interviews into the piece, including clips of her father holding a pistol and her mother's empty and crossed hands. While seated among a large pile of bones, she tried to wash them. The performance took place in Venice in 1997; she remembered the intense heat and that worms emerged from the bones.

Marina Abramović created the performance piece Balkan Baroque in response to the Yugoslav Wars, which took place in the 1990s. The four-day performance earned her the Golden Lion award at the Venice Biennale in 1997. She could not immediately create work about the war due to its personal impact, so she returned to Belgrade, where she interviewed her mother, her father, and a rat-catcher. These interviews were incorporated into the piece, along with clips of her father’s hands holding a pistol and her mother’s empty and later crossed hands. Abramović dressed as a doctor recounting the rat-catcher’s story while sitting among a large pile of bones, attempting to wash them. The performance occurred in Venice in 1997, and she remembered the extreme heat and the emergence of worms from the bones. She explained that scrubbing bones clean is impossible, symbolizing that blood and shame from war cannot be washed away—just as the war cannot be cleansed of its shame. The work was intended to speak not only about the war in Bosnia but about any war anywhere in the world. Beginning on November 9, 2005, Abramović presented Seven Easy Pieces at the Guggenheim Museum in New York City, performing for seven consecutive nights over seven hours, recreating works by five artists from the 1960s and 1970s, including Gina Pane’s The Conditioning and Vito Acconci’s 1972 performance involving masturbation under floorboards, and introducing a new piece on the final night. All performances were dedicated to her late friend Susan Sontag. From March 14 to May 31, 2010, the Museum of Modern Art held a major retrospective of Abramović’s work, curated by Klaus Biesenbach, which was the largest performance art exhibition in MoMA’s history. The exhibition featured the performance The Artist Is Present, which lasted 736 hours and 30 minutes, with Abramović sitting immobile in the atrium while visitors took turns sitting opposite her. Ulay made a surprise appearance at the opening night. She sat in a marked rectangle with a chair opposite her, and visitors were invited to sit and maintain eye contact; most sat for five minutes or less, while a few stayed for a full day. The line grew so large that museum security only noticed it on the last day, when a visitor vomited and another began to disrobe. Tensions arose due to the limited time for earlier visitors. Art enthusiasts speculated about whether Abramović wore an adult diaper, and noted her crying when a sitter cried or during her physical contact with Ulay. She sat across from 1,545 people, including Klaus Biesenbach, James Franco, Lou Reed, Alan Rickman, Jemima Kirke, Jennifer Carpenter, and Björk. A support group, "Sitting with Marina," and a blog, "Marina Abramović made me cry," were established. Marco Anelli took portraits of every sitter, which were published on Flickr, compiled into a book, and exhibited at the Danziger Gallery. Abramović said the show changed her life completely. After Lady Gaga saw and publicized the show, a new audience—particularly young people aged 12 to 18—began attending. In September 2011, a video game version of The Artist Is Present was released by Pippin Barr. In 2013, Dale Eisinger ranked The Artist Is Present ninth in his list of the greatest performance art works. The performance inspired Australian novelist Heather Rose to write The Museum of Modern Love, which was launched at MoMA in 2018. Balkan Erotic Epic is a four-hour durational performance by Abramović, presented at Factory International's Aviva Studios in Manchester from October 9 to 19, 2025, building on her 2005 multi-channel video installation of the same name. The work explores Balkan folklore, collective mythology, ancient myths, ritual, eroticism, spirituality, and tradition, featuring over seventy performers, including dancers, musicians, and singers, and allowing audiences to move freely through thirteen immersive scenes. It includes elements such as Fertility Rite, Massaging the Breast, and Scaring the Gods, re-examining the connection between sexuality, spirituality, and the body in ritual traditions. The performance is noted for its ritualistic use of nudity, multi-space choreography, and focus on reclaiming the body as a site of power and transformation. Frieze described it as a "reclamation, reinvention and perversion of personal and collective history, mythology and identity." The performance is touring in Barcelona (January 24–30, 2026), Berlin (October 14–17, 2026), and New York (December 8–20, 2026). In 2009, Abramović was featured in Chiara Clemente’s documentary Our City Dreams and a book of the same name, which highlighted five artists, including Swoon, Ghada Amer, Kiki Smith, and Nancy Spero, each of whom has a devotion to New York. Abramović is also the subject of the documentary Marina Abramović: The Artist Is Present, based on her 2010 retrospective, which aired on HBO in the United States and won a Peabody Award in 2012. In January 2011, she was on the cover of Serbian ELLE, photographed by Dušan Reljin. Kim Stanley Robinson’s science fiction novel 2312 mentions a performance art style known as "abramovics." In June 2013, a world premiere installation by Abramović was featured at Toronto’s Trinity Bellwoods Park as part of the Luminato Festival, and she co-created the theatrical production The Life and Death of Marina Abramović with Robert Wilson, which premiered at the festival and at the Park Avenue Armory in December. In 2007, Abramović founded the Marina Abramović Institute (MAI), a nonprofit foundation for performance art, in a 33,000-square-foot space in Hudson, New York, and also established a performance institute in San Francisco. She is a patron of the London-based Live Art Development Agency. In June 2014, she presented 512 Hours at London’s Serpentine Gallery, and in December 2014, at the Sean Kelly Gallery in Generator, participants were blindfolded and wore noise-canceling headphones in an exploration of nothingness. On November 30, 2016, to celebrate her 70th birthday, she held a birthday party at the Guggenheim titled "Marina 70," which included a 70-minute "Silence" segment ending with a gong crash, followed by "Entertainment" where she spoke and watched ANOHNI perform "My Way" while wearing a large black hood. In March 2015, she gave a TED talk titled "An art made of trust, vulnerability and connection." In 2019, IFC’s mockumentary show Documentary Now! parodied Abramović’s work and the documentary Marina Abramović: The Artist Is Present, with an episode titled "Waiting for the Artist" starring Cate Blanchett as Isabella Barta (Abramović) and Fred Armisen as Dimo (Ulay). Originally scheduled for September 26, 2020, her first major UK exhibition at the Royal Academy of Arts was postponed to autumn 2021 due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The exhibition, which brought together works spanning her 50-year career and new pieces reflecting on bodily changes and life-death transitions, was described by Tabish Khan of Culture Whisper as "intense, discomfiting, memorable, and performance art at its finest." In 2021, she dedicated a monument titled Crystal Wall of Crying at the site of a Holocaust massacre in Ukraine, at Babi Yar. In 2022, she condemned the Russian invasion of Ukraine. In September 2023, she became the first woman to have a solo exhibition in the Royal Academy’s main galleries, which she helped stage while recovering from a near-fatal pulmonary embolism, exploring how her works might be reinterpreted or reperformed by others using archival footage, installations, and live performances by artists trained in the Marina Abramović Method. In 2026, she is scheduled to have a solo exhibition titled Transforming Energy at Venice’s Gallerie dell'Accademia art biennale, which will be the first exhibition for a living female artist at the museum in its 275-year history. Abramović proposed a performance titled "Come to Wash with Me" in 1969 at Galerija Doma Omladine in Belgrade, where a gallery would be transformed into a laundry with sinks around the walls, and the public would remove their clothes and have them washed, dried, and ironed by Abramović before returning them. The proposal was refused. In 1970, she proposed a similar untitled performance at the same gallery, where she would stand in front of the public dressed in regular clothing, take clothing from a rack (including oversized items like a bra or slip), change into them, and then place a gun to her temple, pulling the trigger—resulting in a possible outcome of her death. Abramović directed a segment titled Balkan Erotic Epic in Destricted, a 2006 compilation of erotic films, and a segment titled Dangerous Games in 2008’s Stories on Human Rights. She also acted in the five-minute short film Antony and the Johnsons: Cut the World. The Marina Abramović Institute (MAI) is a performance art organization focused on performance, long-duration works, and the use of the "Abramović Method." In its early phase, it was a proposed multi-functional museum space in Hudson, New York, designed by Rem Koolhaas and Shohei Shigematsu of OMA, with an early design phase funded by a Kickstarter campaign that raised over 4,000 contributions, including Lady Gaga and Jay-Z. The building project was canceled in October 2017 due to excessive costs. MAI continues as a traveling organization, partnering with institutions and artists internationally in Brazil, Greece, and Turkey. In her youth, she was a performer in one of Hermann Nitsch’s Viennese actionist performances. She maintains a friendship with James Franco, who interviewed her for The Wall Street Journal in 2009, visited her during The Artist Is Present in 2010, and attended the 2012 Met Gala with her. In July 2013, Abramović collaborated with Lady Gaga on the Artpop album, with their work displayed at an event titled "ArtRave" on November 10. They also collaborated on projects supporting MAI, including a video using the Abramović Method and a nonstop reading of Stanisław Lem’s Solaris. In the same month, Jay-Z performed an Abramović-inspired piece at Pace Gallery in New York, performing his track "Picasso Baby" for six straight hours. During the performance, Abramović and several art world figures were invited to dance with him face to face. The footage was used in the music video. She allowed Jay-Z to adapt "The Artist Is Present" under the condition that he would donate to her institute, but stated he did not fulfill this obligation, calling it a "one-way transaction." Two years later, in 2015, she publicly apologized, stating she was never informed of his sizable donation. Abramović claims she feels "neither like a Serb, nor a Montenegrin," but an ex-Yugoslav, saying when asked where she is from, she always says she comes from a country that no longer exists. In February 2025, she endorsed the 2024–2025 Serbian anti-corruption protests. She has had three abortions and has stated that having children would have been a "disaster" for her work. Sculptor Nikola Pešić says she has a lifelong interest in esotericism and spiritualism. Among the Podesta emails was a message from Abramović to Podesta’s brother discussing an invitation to a spirit cooking, which was interpreted by conspiracy theorists.

Abramović describes her identity as neither Serb nor Montenegrin, but as ex-Yugoslav, stating that when asked where she is from, she always says she comes from a country that no longer exists. She claims to have had three abortions in her life and has stated that having children would have been a "disaster" for her work. Sculptor Nikola Pešić notes that Abramović has a lifelong interest in esotericism and spiritualism. In the Podesta emails, a message from Abramović to Podesta's brother about an invitation to a spirit cooking was interpreted by conspiracy theorists like Alex Jones as an invitation to a satanic ritual, and was used as evidence by Jones and others of Hillary Clinton's links to the occult. In a 2013 Reddit Q&A, she clarified that the context determines whether occult practices constitute art: if done in a gallery or artistic context, it is art; otherwise, it is not. On April 10, 2020, Microsoft released a promotional video for HoloLens 2 featuring Abramović, but withdrew it due to accusations from right-wing conspiracy theorists of her having ties to Satanism. Abramović responded by urging people to stop harassing her, emphasizing that her performances are simply the art she has created over the past 50 years. Two years after the initial deal, in 2015, Abramović publicly apologized, stating she was never informed of Jay-Z's sizable donation. In February 2025, she endorsed the 2024–2025 Serbian anti-corruption protests.
